@sfo/aera.name: Aera
@sfo/aera.summary: Cultural/historical name for humanity's perceived structured interaction with reality; not a force, substance, or energy source.

metadata.content: Aera is the human cultural/historical name for structured interaction with reality; not a force, substance, or energy source.

Aera is an ordinary word, not an acronym. It operates through transduction. Lifecycle: Conceive → Shape → Hold → Resolve → Manifest → Release. Aspect is the stabilized energetic structure; manifestation is the event.

@sfo/aera/aspect.name: Aspect
@sfo/aera/aspect.summary: A stabilized energetic structure produced through transduction and shaping.

@sfo/aera/practice.name: Aera Practice
@sfo/aera/practice.summary: Discipline for interacting with reality through transduction.

metadata.content: Kira's Chainmail Robe becomes the Genesis Transductionist symbol. Culture shifts toward understanding Genesis. Binding circle=scaffold, basin=energy, diamond=accessible stored energy, concept=major controllable variable. Better concept improves efficiency/expression and lowers energy cost. @sfo/binding_circle.name: Binding Circle
@sfo/binding_circle.summary: Large circular sigil carved into a fixed surface; its ru’ne geometry and anchor occupancies provide an applied interface for configuring Genesis-field topology.

metadata.content: Binding Circle is a top-level API domain. Checkpoint 5 recovers its foundational internal architecture; the domain remains active and expandable for later detailed applications and circle families.

A Binding Circle is a large sigil physically carved into a floor or other fixed surface, conventionally arranged in a circular footprint. The circle itself is the sigil rather than a container surrounding a separate sigil.

At Blackstone, Genesis Field Studies asks what the Genesis Field is; Binding Circle studies asks what you can build with it.
Binding Circle study is an applied Genesis discipline: the underlying Genesis mathematics already exists, and the circle provides a usable constructed interface for configuring it.

@sfo/cities.name: Cities
@sfo/cities.summary: Stabilized urban nodes organized into capital, large, and small cities, with colored economic districts plus a White civic center.

metadata.content: There are three city classes: Capital Cities, Large Cities, and Small Cities.
Cities are stabilized civilization nodes surrounded by Genesis-stabilized protected territory; beyond that protected territory lies the Wilds.
Colored districts indicate economic availability/luxury level, not poverty or decay.
Every ordinary city has a White civic center associated with the Crown and lower-noble stewardship.
Formal Crown settlement hierarchy: Capital City → Large City → Small City → Village Hub.
Towns exist outside the formal development hierarchy and arise organically from necessity.

@sfo/cities/capital.name: Capital Cities
@sfo/cities/capital.summary: Four Crown/royal-family governed capital cities; each has Red→Violet economic districts plus White civic center.

metadata.content: There are four capital cities in the current kingdom map.
The main capital is governed by the King and Queen.
The other three capitals are governed by members of the royal family: two princes and one princess in the current map assignment.
Capital cities contain Red, Orange, Yellow, Green, Blue, and Violet economic/luxury districts, plus the White civic center.
Current map identifies four capital-city domains by purple/pink, blue, green, and yellow color coding; the primary royal capital is in the purple/pink domain.

@sfo/cities/districts.name: Districts
@sfo/cities/districts.summary: Color-coded economic/luxury districts plus White civic center.

metadata.content: Lowest economic/luxury availability; smaller housing and cheaper businesses, but not inherently impoverished or degraded.
Economic/luxury tier above Red.
Economic/luxury tier above Orange.
Higher economic/luxury tier.
High economic/luxury tier.
Highest economic/luxury tier; opulent/luxury district comparable in feel to a prestige shopping/residential district.
Civic/Crown district, not an economic/luxury tier and not a landed-noble property district.

@sfo/cities/districts/white.name: White Civic District
@sfo/cities/districts/white.summary: Tax-exempt civic/administrative center associated with the Crown and occupied by the lower noble steward family.

metadata.content: White is the municipal/civic center and administrative interface between landed houses and the Crown.
The White civic district does not function as a normal taxed landed district.
The lower noble steward family lives/operates from the White district.
White is associated with Crown authority.
The White civic center collects the Crown's share of district revenues/tribute remitted by upper noble houses.

@sfo/cities/large.name: Large Cities
@sfo/cities/large.summary: Intermediate city class; exact current district ladder remains open pending confirmation.

metadata.content: Large-city district ladder is not yet locked. Current canon leaves the exact highest district color open rather than guessing.

@sfo/cities/permits.name: Municipal Authority & Permitting
@sfo/cities/permits.summary: Citywide construction and civic changes require authorization from the White civic center/lower noble steward acting for the Crown.

metadata.content: Landed ownership does not permit unilateral city construction.
An Orange-ranked noble who wants to build a new structure inside the Orange district must obtain authorization from the White civic center.
The lower noble is responsible for the integrity, engineering, infrastructure, and coordinated operation of the entire city.

@sfo/cities/small.name: Small Cities
@sfo/cities/small.summary: Small city class with Red, Orange, Yellow economic districts plus White civic center.

metadata.content: Small cities contain Red, Orange, and Yellow districts, plus the White civic center.
A small city therefore has three landed upper-noble families—Red, Orange, Yellow—plus one lower-noble steward family in White.
Each landed house manages its district and associated protected holding while the lower noble administers the citywide system.

@sfo/cities/stabilization.name: Genesis Stabilization Network
@sfo/cities/stabilization.summary: Large sigil network that stabilizes the local Genesis Field around a city and surrounding protected domain.

metadata.content: A large sigil network constrains/stabilizes the local Genesis Field around the city and its surrounding protected domain.
Within the effective protected domain, Genesis-field collapse events are suppressed/prevented relative to the Wilds.
A roughly 30-mile-radius protected field has been used as a working example; exact radii should be assigned per mapped city rather than treated as globally fixed.
Genesis stabilization makes permanent estates, vineyards, agriculture, workshops, roads, and other long-term investments viable outside the urban core.
Beyond the protected/stabilized domain, territory transitions into the Wilds.

@sfo/cities/taxation.name: Taxation & Tribute
@sfo/cities/taxation.summary: District-owning upper nobles collect local property-based revenues and remit a Crown-defined share through the White civic center.

metadata.content: Upper nobles collect local property-based revenues from their districts and remit a Crown-defined fraction through the White civic center.
A figure such as 37% has been used illustratively; no canonical percentage is locked yet.
Lower noble compensation comes from Crown-granted city revenue/tax privileges and mine-revenue share rather than ownership of district land.
The Crown receives tribute/revenue shares from the district economy and retains ownership of Genesis mines.

@sfo/cities/town.name: Town
@sfo/cities/town.summary: Emergent necessity-driven settlement that develops along travel routes or other practical nodes outside the formal Crown city-development hierarchy.

metadata.content: Towns sit outside the formal Capital/Large/Small/Village-Hub development hierarchy.
Towns emerge bottom-up from necessity rather than from a Crown city-development program.
Road forks, long travel routes, bridge crossings, passes, ferry points, trade waypoints, or other locations where repeated traffic creates demand.
They act as rest stops/service settlements offering food, lodging, repairs, storage, trade, and other travel necessities.
The Crown may initially pay little administrative attention to small towns.
If a town becomes sufficiently large or economically important, the Crown may eventually tax or regulate it.
A town is emergent; a Village Hub is intentionally established to become a future city.

@sfo/cities/town/emergence.name: Emergent Growth
@sfo/cities/town/emergence.summary: Bottom-up settlement growth from necessity rather than Crown planning.

metadata.content: Repeated practical need → informal services → permanent businesses/residences → emergent town.

@sfo/cities/town/road_network_role.name: Travel-Route Role
@sfo/cities/town/road_network_role.summary: Towns commonly emerge along road junctions, long routes, bridges, passes, ferries, or other repeated travel needs.

metadata.content: Towns help make long-distance road networks survivable by filling service gaps between formal settlements.

@sfo/cities/village_hub.name: Village Hub
@sfo/cities/village_hub.summary: Crown-planned frontier development region and proto-city intended to become a future Small or Large City.

metadata.content: Village Hub is the frontier/proto-city stage beneath Small City in the formal kingdom settlement hierarchy.
A Village Hub exists because the Crown has identified a region worth developing into a future Small or Large City.
Typical frontier-development cycle is approximately 60–80 years.
After the development cycle, a roughly 10-year construction/cannibalization phase converts the region's central hub into the nucleus of the new city.
A Village Hub is intentionally designed to become either a Small City or a Large City.
Village Hubs are Crown-sponsored planned developments, unlike emergent towns.
Village Hub regions are frontier environments in which settlers, guards, surveyors, workers, and institutions gradually stabilize land otherwise exposed to the Wilds.

@sfo/cities/village_hub/center.name: Village Hub Center
@sfo/cities/village_hub/center.summary: Central half-mile or one-mile hub that later becomes the White Civic District of the finished city.

metadata.content: A roughly 0.5 mile × 0.5 mile Village Hub center is intended to become the core of a future Small City.
A roughly 1 mile × 1 mile Village Hub center is intended to become the core of a future Large City.
The Village Hub itself is retained. It becomes the future White Civic District rather than being replaced elsewhere.
The finished city is constructed outward around the original Village Hub center.

@sfo/cities/village_hub/city_transition.name: City Transition
@sfo/cities/village_hub/city_transition.summary: Final construction/cannibalization phase in which the Village Hub becomes the civic nucleus and the city is built outward around it.

metadata.content: Village Hub center → White Civic District → finished city grows outward around it.
The later city-building phase cannibalizes/reorganizes developed parts of the region into permanent urban infrastructure.
The current Kira-region working example uses roughly a 7 mile × 7 mile Small City footprint centered on the old Village Hub.
The finished city does not consume the entire 20-mile-radius development region.
The future city's oldest roads, institutions, families, and local traditions can descend directly from the original Village Hub era.

@sfo/cities/village_hub/development_cycl.name: Development Cycle
@sfo/cities/village_hub/development_cycl.summary: Long Crown-sponsored frontier-development cycle leading to formal city construction.

@sfo/cities/village_hub/development_driv.name: Development Drivers
@sfo/cities/village_hub/development_driv.summary: Strategic/economic reasons the Crown establishes a Village Hub.

metadata.content: A nearby dungeon can justify a Village Hub because of traffic, resources, taxation, and long-term economic value.
A Genesis mine can justify Crown-sponsored development.
A strategically valuable forest or renewable resource domain can justify development.
Travel or logistical value can justify development.
The Crown may establish a Village Hub for any resource, strategic, economic, or geographic reason sufficient to support a future city.

@sfo/cities/village_hub/development_regi.name: Development Region
@sfo/cities/village_hub/development_regi.summary: Larger surveyed/stabilized frontier domain surrounding the Village Hub; not the future city footprint itself.

metadata.content: The current Kira example uses a 20-mile-radius development region.
The development radius is a survey/stabilization/development envelope, not the eventual city footprint.
The region can contain survey zones, guard stations, satellite villages, resource sites, farms, roads, work camps, and other preparatory infrastructure.
The Crown progressively surveys and stabilizes the region so permanent urban development can later exist safely.
The development region represents active Crown expansion into the Wilds.

@sfo/cities/village_hub/frontier_incenti.name: Frontier Incentives
@sfo/cities/village_hub/frontier_incenti.summary: Crown incentives for settlers and workers living in dangerous developing territory.

metadata.content: Frontier settlers can receive tax breaks or reduced taxation.
Extra pay/hazard pay can compensate people for living and working in unstable frontier territory.
Favorable land, business, or development terms can be used to attract settlers and workers.
Incentives make long-duration frontier stabilization economically viable for ordinary families and specialists.

@sfo/cities/village_hub/hollowesmere_exa.name: Kira Village Hub / Hollowesmere Example
@sfo/cities/village_hub/hollowesmere_exa.summary: Current story example: Kira's Village Hub exists because of a nearby dungeon at Hollowesmere.

metadata.content: Kira begins in a Village Hub region whose economic driver is a nearby dungeon.
The current story hub has existed for a couple of decades within its longer development cycle.
The example development region is approximately 20 miles in radius with the Village Hub at the direct center.
Hollowesmere is the dungeon-adjacent settlement/site within the development region.
The central Village Hub eventually becomes the White Civic District of a Small City in the current working example.
Hollowesmere remains outside the main city footprint and can develop into a smaller dungeon-service settlement to reduce congestion from dungeon traffic.
The future city's major revenue stream is expected to come from people traveling there to use/visit the dungeon and its surrounding economy.
Because the development driver is a dungeon, the Village Hub region develops a strong dungeon/Aithren community culture before formal cityhood.

@sfo/cities/village_hub/satellites.name: Satellite Villages & Stations
@sfo/cities/village_hub/satellites.summary: Distributed supporting villages, guard posts, survey sites, camps, and work settlements across the development region.

metadata.content: Satellite nodes can include local villages, guard stations, survey areas, resource camps, work settlements, farms, and other task-specific sites.
They support the larger regional development effort without replacing the Village Hub as the geometric/civic center.
During city formation they may be absorbed, redeveloped, relocated, preserved, or repurposed depending on their position and function.

@sfo/culture/aithren.name: Aithren
@sfo/culture/aithren.summary: Participation-based shared culture associated with dungeon delving and related high-risk Genesis exploration.

metadata.content: Aithren is the native participation-first cultural identity, not generic adventurer. Values include curiosity, experimentation, competence, contribution, trust, information exchange, readiness, humor, belonging. Dungeon-delving Aithren map routes, compare gear, trade discoveries, theorycraft, camp, repair, socialize, and build community. The dungeon is why they arrive; the culture is why they remain.

@sfo/domai.name: Domai
@sfo/domai.summary: Temporary bounded Genesis-field event-landscape with basin identity, anomalous geometry, finite lifespan, resources, elements, and ELDRIS.

metadata.content: A Domai is a temporary bounded Genesis-field environmental event. It is an environment, not a conscious organism.
Domai are basin-classified Red, Orange, Yellow, Green, Blue, or Violet. There is never a White Domai.
Every Domai has a finite lifespan. Red Domai are comparatively short-lived; lifespan increases through the basin ladder, with Violet comparatively long-lived.
A Domai behaves like a continuous chirality knot that eventually loosens/unravels on its own, analogous to a shoelace knot gradually untying.
During its active state, the Domai can sustain anomalous/non-isometric internal geometry and a higher-dimensional-feeling landscape relative to the ordinary exterior.
Active Domai can contain ELDRIS, Genesis crystals, Genesis dust, and fantasy elements.
Voice-to-text 'domain' should normalize to Domai when context clearly refers to this phenomenon.
Conditionally closed for current worldbuilding: core mechanism, lifespan, unraveling, inhabitants/resources/elements established; additional book-facing metadata may be added later.

@sfo/domai/core.name: Superposed White Genesis Crystal
@sfo/domai/core.summary: Non-conscious structural core of every Domai; replaces legacy Heart/Type Zero.

metadata.content: The center/core is a superposed White Genesis Crystal.
The White Genesis Crystal is non-conscious. It does not think, command ELDRIS, or control the Domai as an organism.
The White Genesis Crystal is the introduction/source mechanism for White Genesis dust in MK-147.
Breaking or destroying the White Genesis Crystal forces the Domai into its unraveling phase.
The Domai core is a superposed White Genesis Crystal.
The superposed White Genesis Crystal is non-conscious and functions structurally within the Domai.

@sfo/domai/eldris.name: Domai ELDRIS
@sfo/domai/eldris.summary: ELDRIS manifestations inhabiting/spawning within Domai; replaces legacy Chimera.

metadata.content: ELDRIS do not govern the Domai and are not its consciousness/core.
ELDRIS are hostile manifestations/inhabitants produced or supported by the Domai environment.
ELDRIS are hostile manifestations or inhabitants supported by the Domai environment.
ELDRIS do not govern the Domai and are not its consciousness or core.

@sfo/domai/lifecycle.name: Domai Lifecycle
@sfo/domai/lifecycle.summary: Formation, active lifespan, core break, unraveling, dissipation.

metadata.content: While the White Genesis Crystal remains intact, the Domai persists through its finite natural lifespan unless otherwise disrupted.
If left alone, the continuous chirality-knot structure eventually loosens and the Domai dissipates.
Breaking/destroying the White Genesis Crystal initiates unraveling before natural dissipation.
After core break, anomalous geometry progressively collapses back toward the ordinary local landscape.
Core break triggers a mass-exodus/harvest window: responders rapidly harvest resources and leave before the geometry becomes unsafe or inaccessible.
The unraveling is analogous to a black hole slowly evaporating only as a visualization of progressive disappearance; no Hawking-radiation analogue is implied.
The Domai dissolves back into the normal landscape rather than dying as an organism.

@sfo/domai/resources.name: Domai Resources
@sfo/domai/resources.summary: Genesis crystals and Genesis dust produced/harvested within Domai.

metadata.content: Genesis crystals occur within Domai and are harvestable.
Genesis dust occurs within Domai; White Genesis dust is specifically associated with the superposed White Genesis Crystal/core mechanism.
Unraveling creates a high-risk final harvesting period before evacuation.

@sfo/domai/responders.name: Domai Aithren
@sfo/domai/responders.summary: Aithren branch specializing in entering active Domai; native subgroup name pending.

metadata.content: This is the Aithren branch informally remembered as storm chasers: specialists who enter active Domai rather than persistent dungeons.
Native subgroup name remains open; 'storm chasers' is descriptive author shorthand, not locked world terminology.

@sfo/domai/response.name: Domai Response
@sfo/domai/response.summary: Authority/responder escalation by Domai basin class.

metadata.content: Red Domai are handled locally. The Crown/kingdom military does not automatically respond; response is left to local nobility, Aithren Domai specialists/storm-chaser culture, and other local resources.

Orange Domai are still handled locally. The Crown/kingdom military does not automatically respond; nobility and Aithren Domai specialists manage the event unless local conditions require something exceptional.
Yellow is the threshold basin. A Yellow Domai receives a kingdom military response.
Green Domai receive kingdom military response.
Blue Domai receive kingdom military response.
Violet Domai receive kingdom military response.
Military escalation rule: Red/Orange = local/nobility/Aithren response; Yellow/Green/Blue/Violet = kingdom military also responds.
Red and Orange Domai are considered manageable enough that they are not automatically treated as kingdom-wide military incidents.

@sfo/dungeon.summary: Geographic Genesis-field domain with basin-separated environmental regions and associated culture.

metadata.content: Persistent geographic Genesis-field structure; environment separates Genesis into basin-dominant domains like a prism; basin-native monsters are gated from incompatible domains; exterior camps can be safe; dungeons oscillate/regenerate/produce resources and crystals; deeper domains create environmental exposure whose exact mitigation remains unresolved.

@sfo/evil/bandits.name: Bandits
@sfo/evil/bandits.summary: Persistent decentralized criminal groups operating through ambush, theft, kidnapping, extortion, and unsafe-road control.

metadata.content: Bandits are a persistent travel and logistics threat: road obstructions, ambushes, night raids, kidnapping for ransom, theft of cargo, and supply disruption.
Bandit settlements are small hidden camps/towns designed to be temporary, relocatable, camouflaged, and difficult to locate.
Bandit camps rotate locations in response to local environmental danger and external pressure; abandoned camps may remain intact for years.
Bandits force caravans and travelers to hire guards, plan routes, and treat long-distance movement as an operational problem.
Bounties can be issued by local authorities, merchant coalitions, or noble houses; specialized hunters target leaders, camps, supply routes, and infrastructure.
Bandits maintain road danger and recurring local antagonism without requiring every journey to become a war.

Bandits primarily operate from the Wilds, using overgrowth, sparse authority, temporary settlements, and mobility to avoid suppression.
Bandits prey on travelers moving between cities and village hubs along roads crossing the Wilds.
Bandit groups can move their camps through the Wilds rather than depending on permanent settlements.
Persistent nuisance threat in the Wilds and along long-distance travel corridors; especially dangerous to caravans and travelers.
Bandits force travelers to plan logistics, hire guards, travel in groups, and treat roads through the Wilds as operationally dangerous.
Road obstructions, ambushes, night raids, kidnapping for ransom, and theft of cargo and supplies.
Small hidden camps or towns in the Wilds; temporary, relocatable, camouflaged, and deliberately difficult to locate.
Settlements can rotate location in response to external pressure and local Genesis conditions; abandoned camps may remain intact for long periods.
Bandit-hunting is supported by standing bounties issued by authorities, merchant interests, and noble houses.
Counter-bandit operations target leaders, camps, supply routes, and supporting infrastructure.
Maintains road danger and recurring travel pressure without requiring every journey to become a major war.
Bandits are native operators of the Wilds rather than city-based sovereign powers.

@sfo/aera/transcription/pssp.name: Phase State Shadow Projection (PSSP)
@sfo/aera/transcription/pssp.summary: Realization projection that expands a bound latent phase-state inherited by a Genesis identity into its active persistent shadow manifold; the manifold is the admissible structural scaffold into which basin-conditioned energy is organized prior to conscious shaping.

metadata.content: PSSP realizes a bound phase-state as the persistent Genesis manifold that defines the admissible structural corridors into which basin-conditioned energy may be organized prior to conscious shaping.
metadata.source: PSSP v0.1 formalization — ratified by Genesis 2026-09-01

metadata.content: Working operator: PSSP_(D,B,R) : Adm(K) ⇀ Man(D), with M = PSSP_(D,B,R)(s).
PSSP is not the Binding Circle. Binding makes the latent phase-state part of the practitioner's admissible inherited identity; PSSP accesses and expands/projects that state into the active manifold.
The PSSP output is the shadow manifold/scaffold, not yet the final manifested shaping.
PSSP uses realization projection terminology. It must not be silently identified with the generic dimension-reducing PROJECT operation in the Genesis morphism firewall.

Genesis Point described PSSP as projecting an underlying phase structure into a persistent phase shadow; the old literal lattice/higher-dimensional language is preserved historically while the current MK-147 mechanism is typed in Genesis-field terms.

@sfo/aera/transcription/pssp/phase_state.name: Bound Phase State
@sfo/aera/transcription/pssp/phase_state.summary: Compact/latent admissible configuration inherited by a Genesis identity after Binding and available for later PSSP realization.

metadata.content: A bound phase-state s belongs to Adm(K): the admissible configuration space of the practitioner's closed Genesis identity.
Author-facing model: the compact spiky ball is the latent bound phase-state. It is part of Kira's admissible inherited identity but is not yet the expanded active manifold.
Binding can enlarge/reconfigure Kira's admissible inherited state-set while Kira remains Kira under the relevant Genesis identity relation.

@sfo/aera/transcription/pssp/shadow_mani.name: Phase-State Shadow Manifold
@sfo/aera/transcription/pssp/shadow_mani.summary: Active expanded Genesis manifold produced by PSSP from a bound phase-state; it is the structural scaffold that specifies permissible corridors for later energy organization.

metadata.content: For a bound state s, M = PSSP_(D,B,R)(s) is the active shadow manifold.
Author-facing model: PSSP expands/projects the compact spiky ball into the sphere/manifold scaffold.
The manifold says which structural paths are permissible. Energy does not create the topology; energy is organized into/through the already-realized scaffold.
The older Genesis Point source defined 'shadow' as a persistent projected field/effect rather than absence of light.

@sfo/aera/transcription/pssp/corridor_ar.name: PSSP Corridor Architecture
@sfo/aera/transcription/pssp/corridor_ar.summary: Internal corridor/incidence organization of the shadow manifold; each corridor carries structural basin requirements and stabilization conditions.

metadata.content: Working manifold tuple: M=(X_M, C_M, I_M, b_M, S_M), with carrier, corridor set, incidence organization, basin-requirement map, and stabilization-condition map.
The corridor architecture is a construction specification for the shaping manifold.

@sfo/aera/transcription/pssp/basin_signa.name: PSSP Basin Signature
@sfo/aera/transcription/pssp/basin_signa.summary: Structural specification of which Genesis energy basins are required by the corridors of a particular shadow manifold; basin membership is not a power ranking.

metadata.content: For each corridor c∈C_M, b_M(c) specifies one or more required basins from the ordinary basin alphabet {R,O,Y,G,B,V}.
BasinSig(M)=⋃_(c∈C_M) b_M(c).
If a Fireball manifold requires Red, Orange, and Green, BasinSig(M_F)={R,O,G}. This describes structural construction requirements, not how powerful the Fireball is.
Basin choice is analogous to a carpenter selecting a 2×4 versus a 4×4 because the frame requires that structural member; the choice is about construction, not an abstract power tier.

@sfo/aera/transcription/pssp/stabilizati.name: PSSP Corridor Stabilization
@sfo/aera/transcription/pssp/stabilizati.summary: Energy-density admissibility conditions under which every required corridor of a realized shadow manifold remains structurally stabilized.

metadata.content: For each corridor c, an energy-density assignment e_c must lie within that corridor's admissible stabilization region S_M(c).
The shadow manifold is energetically stabilized only when every required corridor satisfies its local stabilization condition.
Energy density is used to stabilize the required corridor architecture. Basin identity remains structural and does not encode a basin power hierarchy.

@sfo/aera/transcription/pssp/shaping_han.name: PSSP Shaping Handoff
@sfo/aera/transcription/pssp/shaping_han.summary: Handoff from an energetically stabilized shadow manifold to the practitioner's conscious shaping operation, which resolves/collapses the energized scaffold into the operative manifested shaping.

metadata.content: Binding → bound phase-state → PSSP shadow manifold → basin-conditioned energy occupancy/stabilization → conscious shaping.
Working shaping handoff: Shape_(K,Q) : (M,E) ⇀ Y, defined for a stabilized manifold/energy configuration.
Phase State ≠ Shadow Manifold ≠ Energy Occupancy ≠ Manifested Shaping.

@sfo/aera/transcription/pssp/failure_mod.name: PSSP Failure Modes
@sfo/aera/transcription/pssp/failure_mod.summary: Failure conditions for realization or stabilization when the bound state cannot lawfully resolve into the requested manifold or its required corridors cannot be maintained.

metadata.content: PSSP is undefined when the requested manifold is not reachable under the current domain/Bandwidth, fails the required identity invariants, is not distinguishable at the operative Resolution, or fails closure.
A realized manifold can still fail operationally if one or more required corridor energy assignments lie outside their admissible stabilization regions.
